entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gérard du Puy (died February 22, 1389) was a French cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church, a prominent figure during the tumultuous Avignon Papacy and the initial phase of the Great Western Schism. Elevated to cardinal by his uncle, Pope Gregory XI, in 1375, du Puy's career exemplifies the political and familial networks that shaped the late medieval Church, particularly during its period of residence in Avignon. His influence stemmed not only from his familial connection to the pontiff but also from his administrative acumen, positioning him as a key advisor and diplomat within the papal Curia.

Prior to his cardinalate, Gérard du Puy served as the Abbot of Marmoutier, a significant Benedictine monastery in France, and held various curial positions, demonstrating his experience in ecclesiastical administration. His elevation to cardinal-priest of San Clemente on December 20, 1375, marked a peak in his career. Following Gregory XI's return to Rome in 1377 and subsequent death, du Puy participated in the contentious conclave of 1378 that elected Urban VI, an election he, along with many other cardinals, later repudiated. This repudiation led to the election of Antipope Clement VII and the commencement of the Great Western Schism.

Throughout the schism, Gérard du Puy remained a steadfast supporter of the Avignon line, serving Clement VII as a trusted advisor and administrator. His continued presence and counsel lent legitimacy and administrative stability to the Avignon court, contributing to the schism's entrenched nature. He played a role in diplomatic efforts to secure support for Clement VII among European monarchs, particularly in France, which remained a staunch ally of the Avignon papacy, further entrenching the division of Christendom.

entities.summary:
Gérard du Puy was a French cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church and cardinal-nephew of Pope Gregory XI.

Born in France around 1320, Gérard rose to prominence within the papal court through his close relationship with the Pope. This position granted him significant influence over church policies and allowed him to shape the religious landscape of Western Europe during the late medieval period. Du Puy's tenure as cardinal spanned nearly three decades, during which he played a key role in several high-profile ecclesiastical events.

Du Puy's legacy is marked by his involvement in the papal conclave that elected Pope Gregory XII in 1409, which led to the Avignon Papacy and ultimately contributed to the Western Schism. His influence also extended to the French monarchy, where he served as a trusted advisor to King Charles VI.

Du Puy's contributions to the Catholic Church were not limited to his role as cardinal; he was also a skilled diplomat who helped negotiate several important treaties between European powers.

Gérard du Puy died on February 22, 1389, at the age of around 69, leaving behind a lasting impact on the history of the Roman Catholic Church.

Du Puy's story serves as a reminder of the complex web of relationships and power dynamics that shaped medieval European politics and religion.
